paras: The ducking of a Black woman at Edinburg, Virginia, was an assault in the summer of 1895 in which a woman from Woodstock was ducked in Stony Creek and ordered to leave the town within three days. She left, and the only known report, a paragraph in the Edinburg column of the Woodstock Shenandoah Herald, approved of the outcome.

According to the Herald's Edinburg correspondent, the woman came from Woodstock and had been employed at Edinburg for some weeks. The correspondent did not name her, referring to her only by the slur "coon," and charged that she "had passed herself off as a widow."

She was ducked in Stony Creek "on account of her misconduct," in the column's words, and then notified to leave the place within three days. The paragraph is written in the passive voice and does not say who ducked her, how many took part, or when it happened, beyond appearing in the issue of August 23, 1895.
The woman "wisely took warning and left," the correspondent wrote. No report of an arrest or any legal action appears in the coverage.

The episode survives in a single item among the Herald's "Edinburg Items," set between a note on a baseball victory over Mount Jackson and an account of a night attack on a local woman, Mrs. Proctor, by a man disguised in blackface. The correspondent treated the ducking as deserved local news, naming the woman by a slur and closing with "May she never come back." No other white paper and no Black paper was found to have reported it.
